# Preface {.unnumbered}

**Arisbe** offers an environment for *doing logic in pictures, not pictures of logic*. It
makes Charles Sanders Peirce's "moving pictures of thought" operational, with Frithjof
Dau's formalization standing as the guarantor of correctness.

The system exists to solve one central engineering and research problem: the **inerrant
correspondence between an existential graph's linear written form and its graphical drawn
form**. Picture and proposition must denote the same mathematical object across every
transformation, every layout, every edit, every round-trip. That contract forms the book's
spine; Part I gives it its own chapter, and Part IV treats it in depth.

## How this book is organized

The book follows the [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr) shape so that one source can serve both
a linear read and task-oriented lookup:

- **I · Why** — what Arisbe is, the central problem, and the philosophy underneath it.
- **II · Getting started** — install and run it from the repository, draw your first graph,
  find the door that fits your background, and (for scholars) read the research invitation.
- **III · Using Arisbe** — the three modes in practice, the worked examples, and
  import/export including the Peirce-edition publishing path.
- **IV · How it works** — the architecture, the correspondence contract in depth, and a map
  of what is built.
- **V · Reference** — linear formats, the core API, the glossary, and prior art.

## One source, two renders

This book comes from the project's own documentation, built with
[Quarto](https://quarto.org). The same source renders to:

- a **browseable web help** (an HTML site, also served in-app — see *Install & run*), and
- a **book** (PDF and epub).

The reader chapters consist of the canonical docs that live under `docs/`, selected and
ordered here. The project's design-of-record, roadmap, and session notes stay in the
repository; the reader's book deliberately excludes them.

> **New here?** Jump to **II · Getting started → Install & run**, then **Your first graph**.
